## Why This Matters

The spam filter is the first machine-learning system most people ever touched. A text message is just
a pile of words; the filter has read thousands of past messages, each labeled *spam* or *not*. How
does counting words turn into a verdict on a brand-new message?

The answer is the algorithm in this lesson. Naive Bayes keeps every piece of the machinery from L06 —
Bayes' rule, the prior, the MAP decision — and adds one bold shortcut that lets the same recipe scale
from two mango measurements to the **tens of thousands of word-features** of a document. That shortcut
is wrong, in a way we will make precise, and the classifier works astonishingly well anyway.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
Picture a juror who weighs each piece of testimony *on its own* — "how typical is this clue of a
guilty defendant? of an innocent one?" — and then multiplies the suspicions, clue after clue, never
asking whether the witnesses might be repeating each other. Fast, a little credulous, and in practice
uncannily effective. That juror is Naive Bayes; the credulity is the *naive* assumption.
:::

## From a Full Model to a Naive One

L06 built a generative classifier by Bayes' rule: to label a point $\mathbf{x}$, compare the classes
on **prior times likelihood** and pick the largest — the MAP rule,

$$\text{predict } \underset{C}{\text{argmax}} \; P(C)\, P(\mathbf{x} \mid C).$$

GDA modeled the likelihood $P(\mathbf{x} \mid C)$ as one **multivariate** Gaussian per class, covariance
and all, so it captured how the features move *together* (longer mangoes weigh more). That richness has
a price. With many features the likelihood is the probability of the *whole combination at once*, and a
modest 30 yes/no features already make $2^{30} \approx$ a billion combinations — almost none of which
your training set has ever seen. For text, with one feature per vocabulary word, the combination space
is astronomical. Estimating a likelihood per combination is hopeless.

Naive Bayes breaks the deadlock with one simplification: **assume the features are conditionally
independent given the class.** Then the joint likelihood *factors* into a product of one-feature
likelihoods —

$$P(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_p \mid C) = \prod_{k=1}^{p} P(x_k \mid C).$$

Each feature's likelihood is now estimated *separately* — count it, or fit a one-feature distribution —
and the pieces just multiply. In L06's language: **erase the off-diagonal covariance.** GDA's full
covariance matrix becomes a diagonal one; the model stops tracking correlations and looks at each
feature alone. That is the whole idea. The assumption is called *naive* because real features do
correlate; the surprise, confirmed in the lab, is how little the classifier seems to mind.

## Counting Likelihoods: Does the League Play?

When features are categorical, the per-feature likelihoods are just **counts**. The Humacao beach
volleyball league's last 12 scheduled days, by weather:

| Weather | Played? | | Weather | Played? |
|---------|---------|-|---------|---------|
| sunny | yes | | sunny | yes |
| sunny | yes | | overcast | yes |
| sunny | yes | | overcast | no |
| overcast | yes | | rainy | no |
| overcast | yes | | rainy | no |
| rainy | yes | | sunny | no |

Today is **rainy** — does the league play? Count what you need: the league played on 8 of 12 days
($P(\text{yes}) = 8/12$) and skipped 4 ($P(\text{no}) = 4/12$); among the 8 played days exactly 1 was
rainy ($P(\text{rainy} \mid \text{yes}) = 1/8$); among the 4 skipped days, 2 were rainy
($P(\text{rainy} \mid \text{no}) = 2/4$). Then prior times likelihood, per class:

$$P(\text{yes}) \cdot P(\text{rainy} \mid \text{yes}) = \tfrac{8}{12} \cdot \tfrac{1}{8} = \tfrac{1}{12} \approx 0.083$$
$$P(\text{no}) \cdot P(\text{rainy} \mid \text{no}) = \tfrac{4}{12} \cdot \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{1}{6} \approx 0.167$$

The "no" score wins — MAP says the league stays home — and normalizing the two scores so they sum to 1
gives honest posteriors: $P(\text{no} \mid \text{rainy}) = 2/3$, $P(\text{yes} \mid \text{rainy}) = 1/3$.
With a single feature the naive assumption never had to fire; add a second column (was it a holiday?)
and its likelihood would simply *join the product* — that is the entire upgrade, and it is exactly what
the lab does at scale with thousands of word-columns.

## The Zero-Frequency Problem and Laplace Smoothing

Imagine a record in which the league had *never* skipped a sunny day (our 12-day table has one such
day, so really $P(\text{sunny} \mid \text{no}) = 1/4$; suppose instead it were $0/4$). Today is sunny.
That single zero would annihilate the entire "no" product — one unseen combination vetoes the class
outright, no matter how strong the other evidence. In text this happens constantly: a word that never
appeared in the spam training set would veto *spam* for any message containing it.

The standard fix is **Laplace smoothing** (add-one smoothing): add one phantom count to every cell, so
no estimated probability is ever exactly zero. It is cheap insurance, on by default as a tunable
`alpha` in scikit-learn's count-based Naive Bayes. The lab shows a message whose verdict *flips* when
smoothing is turned on — one unseen word vetoes a class to zero without it.

## Continuous Features: Gaussian Naive Bayes

Lengths and weights have no cells to count. **Gaussian Naive Bayes** replaces each count-based
likelihood with a normal density: for each class and each feature, fit a Gaussian to that class's
training values — just a mean and a standard deviation — then read $P(x_k \mid C)$ off that bell curve.
Everything else — priors, the product, MAP — is unchanged.

This is precisely **GDA with a diagonal covariance**. L06's LDA and QDA fit a *full* covariance per
class and so model the length-weight tilt; Gaussian Naive Bayes fits only the per-feature variances and
assumes the tilt away. On the mangoes, whose two features really are correlated, that costs a couple of
points of accuracy — you measure exactly how much in the lab. The naive assumption is not free; it is
just often cheap.

## Text Classification: Where Naive Bayes Earns Its Living

Text is the application that made this algorithm famous, and it is where the independence assumption
stops being a liability and becomes the only thing that makes the problem tractable.

First, turn a document into numbers. The **bag of words** representation builds a vocabulary from the
training messages and counts how many times each word appears in each message — one feature per word,
order discarded. A corpus of a few hundred short messages already has a vocabulary of a few hundred
words, so every message becomes a vector with hundreds of features, almost all of them zero. Modeling
the *joint* distribution over hundreds of word-counts is the combinatorial wall again; the naive
assumption walks through it by treating each word as an independent vote.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  D["a new message:<br/>'free prize claim now'"] --> W["bag of words:<br/>free=1 prize=1 claim=1 now=1"]
  W --> S["P(word | spam) for each word<br/>times the spam prior"]
  W --> H["P(word | ham) for each word<br/>times the ham prior"]
  S --> M["compare the two products"]
  H --> M
  M --> V["MAP verdict:<br/>spam or ham"]
```

With counts as features, the right variant is **multinomial Naive Bayes**: the per-word likelihood
$P(\text{word} \mid C)$ is estimated as that word's share of all words in the class's training messages
(Laplace-smoothed), and a message's class score multiplies in one factor per word it contains. Training
is just counting, so it finishes essentially instantly even on enormous corpora.

Why did Naive Bayes dominate spam filtering for years? Spam is its perfect storm: tens of thousands of
word-count features (independence is wrong but workable), heavy class imbalance handled naturally by the
prior, training fast enough to personalize per user, and updates as cheap as recounting. The lab builds
a small spam filter, reads off the words it found most spam-like, and reproduces one of its verdicts by
hand.

## The Naive Bayes Family

"Naive Bayes" is a recipe, not a single model: pick the per-feature likelihood that matches your data.

| Variant | Per-feature likelihood | Use it for |
|---------|------------------------|-----------|
| **GaussianNB** | a normal density (mean, standard deviation) | continuous features (lengths, weights) |
| **MultinomialNB** | a word's share of the class's counts | counts — text, bag of words |
| **BernoulliNB** | present-or-absent probability | binary features (did the word occur at all) |

Same Bayes' rule, same MAP, same independence assumption — only the likelihood changes.

## Naive Bayes Among the Classifiers

Naive Bayes sits on the **generative** side of the split L05 named: it models what each class *looks
like* — $P(\mathbf{x} \mid C)$ and $P(C)$ — and lets Bayes' rule produce the boundary, where logistic
regression (L04) and the Perceptron (L05) model the boundary $P(C \mid \mathbf{x})$ directly.

| | Generative (Naive Bayes, GDA) | Discriminative (logistic) |
|---|------------------------------|---------------------------|
| Learns | what each class *looks like* | what *separates* the classes |
| Models | $P(\mathbf{x} \mid C)$ and $P(C)$ | $P(C \mid \mathbf{x})$ directly |
| Training | counting / means and spreads — instant | iterative gradient descent |
| Strength | tiny data, many features, text | calibrated probabilities, correlated features |

And within the generative family, Naive Bayes is GDA's thrifty cousin: GDA spends parameters on a full
covariance and captures correlations; Naive Bayes drops them for speed and scale. Use the full model
when features are few and correlated; use the naive one when they are many and cheap to count.

## When to Use / When NOT to Use

- **Use it when:** features are counts or categories (text!); training data is scarce (per-feature
  means and counts stabilize on a handful of examples); you need a model trained and serving in
  milliseconds; you want a fast, honest baseline before anything fancier.
- **Avoid it when:** features are strongly redundant (ten copies of one signal get multiplied as ten
  independent witnesses — overconfidence by construction); or you need well-calibrated probabilities
  rather than a good argmax.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Reading Naive Bayes probabilities as calibrated.** The independence shortcut double-counts
  correlated evidence, so posteriors crowd toward 0 and 1 — you will watch one pin to $1.000$ in the
  lab. The *ranking* (which class wins) survives; the exact $0.98$ should not be quoted to a
  decision-maker without a calibration check (Unit III).
- **Forgetting smoothing with count data.** One unseen word-class pair should not veto a class; that is
  what Laplace smoothing is for.
- **Dismissing it for its assumption.** "Features are never independent" is true and beside the point —
  Naive Bayes is the canonical example of a wrong model that predicts well, and a wrong-but-fast
  baseline is often exactly what the moment needs.

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: why implementations sum logs (Optional)" collapse="true"}
A text classifier multiplies *thousands* of per-word likelihoods, and the product underflows to exactly
$0.0$ in floating point long before the end. Every real implementation therefore works with logarithms:
maximize $\log P(C) + \sum_k \log P(x_k \mid C)$, a sum of moderate negative numbers, which is
monotonically equivalent to maximizing the product — the MAP winner is identical. The lab's by-hand
computation does exactly this, comparing two log-scores like $-21.6$ and $-35.9$, and matches
scikit-learn's `predict_log_proba`. The habit is worth copying: when probabilities multiply, sum logs.
:::

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Naive Bayes or logistic regression — which do I try first?"** Professionals often run both; they
cost minutes. Reach for Naive Bayes first when data is small, features are counts or text, or you need
a trained model *now*; prefer logistic regression when you have data to spare and the probabilities
themselves matter. The lab stages this exact comparison on a bag of words.

**"If the independence assumption is false, why trust the answer?"** Because classification only needs
the *ranking* of the class scores to be right, not their exact values. Correlated evidence skews the
magnitudes — that is the overconfidence — but usually leaves the winner unchanged. A wrong model can
still make the right call.

**"Why did Naive Bayes dominate spam filtering for years?"** Tens of thousands of word features, class
imbalance the prior handles for free, training fast enough to personalize per user, and updates as
cheap as recounting. The first mass-deployed ML system most people ever touched was this lesson's
algorithm reading their inbox.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Naive assumption | features independent given the class; per-feature likelihoods multiply |
| Why it is needed | the full joint over many features is unestimable (combinatorial wall) |
| In L06's terms | Naive Bayes is GDA with the off-diagonal covariance erased (diagonal) |
| Count likelihoods | $P(\text{feature} \mid C)$ from counts; the volleyball table |
| Laplace smoothing | add phantom counts so no unseen value vetoes a class to zero |
| Gaussian NB | per-class, per-feature normal densities — continuous features |
| Multinomial NB | per-word count shares — text, bag of words |
| Overconfidence | independence double-counts correlated evidence; ranking survives, calibration does not |
